title: Overview of the TREC 2008 Legal Track
author: Douglas W. Oard · Bruce Hedin · Stephen Tomlinson · Jason R. Baron

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: E-discovery evidence: Manual review is no gold standard
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified proposition: several automated retrieval runs outperformed a negotiated Boolean baseline, while attorney involvement, relevance-assessment uncertainty, and benchmark realism constrain any claim of universal machine superiority or automatic legal defensibility.

While some compromise on realism is always going to be required if a task is to enable valid approach-to-approach comparisons, we have endeavored, in this year’s Interactive Task, to model as closely as possible the conditions and objectives of real-world responsive review.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source provides foundational e-discovery evidence consistent with selective, human-led deployment: performance varies by retrieval method and context, attorney interaction materially shapes effectiveness, and manual assessment requires quality control and adjudication. It supports task-specific evaluation and meaningful oversight, though it does not address generative AI or broader labour and operating-model effects.

kp.k: E-discovery benchmarking targets recall and affordable human review
kp.d: This 2008 study evaluates information retrieval for litigation and regulatory discovery, rather than generative AI. Its three tasks—Ad Hoc, Relevance Feedback and Interactive—compare automatic, two-pass and interactive retrieval. The operational objective is to return document sets for subsequent human review, balancing exhaustive evidence retrieval against unnecessary review costs. Fifteen research teams participated in 2008, using a tobacco-document collection containing 6,910,192 records.
qs: TREC 2008 was the third year of the Legal Track, which focuses on evaluation of search technology for discovery of electronically stored information in litigation and regulatory settings.
This year, there were a total of 15 participating research teams.
The IIT CDIP 1.0 collection consists of 6,910,192 document records in the form of XML elements.

kp.k: Operational evaluation requires choosing document-production thresholds
kp.d: The Ad Hoc and Relevance Feedback tasks introduced balanced F1 and participant-selected retrieval thresholds to model the practical obligation to return bounded document sets. Threshold selection remained difficult: the best Ad Hoc mean F1 run set K to the maximum 100,000 for every topic. Estimated relevant documents averaged 82,403 per topic, and six topics exceeded the submission ceiling, limiting the ability to test thresholding adequately.
qs: It also modeled a real operational requirement of e-discovery systems to return a set of documents, not just an unbounded ranked list.
The highest scoring run in mean F1 @K (wat7fuse) just set K=100,000 (the maximum allowed) for all topics, which probably isn’t a generally applicable thresholding approach.
Unfortunately, six of the topics had more than 100,000 relevant documents, i.e., more relevant documents than the participant runs were allowed to retrieve for a topic.

kp.k: Automated retrieval exceeded Boolean baselines, with unresolved explanations
kp.d: Five of ten Ad Hoc teams submitted runs exceeding the final negotiated Boolean baseline on mean F1 at their chosen thresholds; seven exceeded it on mean Recall@B. The final Boolean run averaged 24% recall and 16% F1. The authors explicitly decline to attribute improved relative performance solely to threshold flexibility or technological progress: broader topics, altered Boolean construction and natural variation in human negotiation remain possible explanations.
qs: Five of the 10 participating research teams submitted a run of higher mean F1 @K than the reference Boolean run
7 of the 10 participating research teams actually submitted a run of higher mean Recall@B than the reference Boolean run in 2008.
This year, the average recall of the final negotiated Boolean query was 24%, close to last year’s average recall of 22%.
More analysis is needed to understand this result.

kp.k: Boolean searching missed materially important documents
kp.d: The new highly relevant category sought to distinguish material or hot documents from merely relevant records. Across applicable topics, the original consensus Boolean query retrieved an estimated 42% of highly relevant documents, leaving 58% unretrieved; the final negotiated query averaged 33% recall of highly relevant documents. These are distinct negotiation stages. The authors caution that the category lacked training data and its inter-annotator agreement had not yet been studied.
qs: A second major change this year was the introduction of a “highly relevant” category for relevance assessment, modeling the legal concept of evidence being “material” rather than merely relevant.
It is not yet clear how useful this new category will be, in part because we have yet to study inter-annotator agreement for this assessment task.
For highly relevant documents, the average recall of the final negotiated Boolean query was 33%.
58% of the “highly relevant” documents were not found by the consensus Boolean query

kp.k: Sampling makes evaluation feasible but introduces substantial uncertainty
kp.d: Ad Hoc evaluation used probability-weighted samples from pooled runs, with typically 500 judgments per topic. Twenty-seven topics received 14,771 judgments; 26 supported all-relevant evaluation and 24 supported highly relevant evaluation. Recall estimation assumed relevance did not extend beyond the pool, an assumption explored through random sampling. The authors warn of substantial topic-level estimation errors and suggest that averages across topics are more reliable. Random-run findings could also reflect assessor false positives rather than genuinely missed relevance.
qs: Affordable evaluation of large result sets requires sampling and estimation.
In total, 14,771 judgments were produced for the 27 topics.
These C values are fairly low, indicating that substantial estimation errors are possible on individual topics.
Mean scores (over 24 or 26 topics) should be somewhat more reliable than the estimates for individual topics.
The random reference run allows us to separately analyze the accuracy of this assumption.

kp.k: Feedback benefits were limited by thresholding and inconsistent judgments
kp.d: Five teams submitted 29 Relevance Feedback runs, with 12 evaluated topics and nine supporting highly relevant evaluation. Previously judged documents were excluded from scoring to test discovery of new relevant records. The median feedback run scored below the median baseline on mean F1; the Boolean reference achieved the highest mean F1@Kr for all relevant documents. A small consistency study reported only 58% of previously relevant documents judged relevant again and 18% of previously non-relevant documents newly judged relevant. The authors identify assessor variation, sampling, pooling differences and possibly OCR as unresolved contributors.
qs: A total of 5 research teams submitted 29 runs for this year’s Relevance Feedback task.
Furthermore, the median feedback run actually scored lower in mean F1 than the median baseline run.
However, the number of topics is small.
We see that just 58% of previously judged relevant documents were judged relevant again this year
18% of previously judged non-relevant documents were judged relevant this year

kp.k: Attorney-defined relevance anchors the interactive retrieval workflow
kp.d: The redesigned Interactive task assigned an attorney Topic Authority to define responsiveness, clarify ambiguous requests, guide assessors and adjudicate appeals. Teams could use up to ten hours of authority time per topic and had to classify the entire collection as relevant or not relevant. The model treats technology and review teams as implementing the responsible attorney’s conception of responsiveness, including substantive and case-strategy considerations, rather than independently resolving every possible interpretation.
qs: The review team is not asked to consider, weigh, and resolve differences between all possible conceptions of relevance
Each team could ask for up to 10 hours of a Topic Authority’s time for purposes of clarifying a topic.

Teams were of course free to use relevance ranking as a means to arrive at their result sets, but the final deliverable was a single binary classification (relevant/not relevant) of the full population of documents.
The final decision on all appeals rested with the Topic Authority.

kp.k: Attorney interaction correlated with stronger retrieval effectiveness
kp.d: On Topic 103, H5 used 485 minutes of Topic Authority time and achieved post-adjudication recall of 0.624, precision of 0.810 and F1 of 0.705, compared with the pooled Ad Hoc F1 of 0.392. Among active participants, the reported correlation between clarification time and F1 was 0.927, with a 95% confidence interval of (0.577, 0.989). The authors note few observations, no middle-range interaction times, differing resources and unresolved effects of retrieval methods versus clarification. This is an association from a small exercise, not an isolated causal estimate of attorney interaction.
qs: one team (Pittsburgh) used just 5 of their permitted 600 Topic Authority minutes, while another (H5) used 485 minutes.
we obtain a Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient of 0.927 with a 95% confidence interval of (0.577, 0.989).
we would expect that there are some approaches to gathering the required information that work better than others.
This is a question that merits further study.

kp.k: Appeals exposed consequential errors in human relevance assessment
kp.d: Across the three Interactive topics, participants appealed 966 first-pass assessments; Topic Authorities overturned 762, or 78.9%, and maintained 204, or 21.1%. Topic 103 accounted for 950 appeals. Adjudication increased all active participants’ Topic 103 F1 scores but did not alter submission rankings on any topic. Appeals were restricted to contradictions of prior guidance or apparent inconsistencies, and authorities knew which teams submitted them. The findings concern quality control of human assessment, not a measured generative-model error rate.
qs: In all, 966 assessments were appealed (aggregating across all three topics).

Of these, the Topic Authority agreed with the appealing team (or teams; there were some cases of overlapping appeals) on 762 (78.9%); the Topic Authority denied the appeal (maintained the first-pass assessment) on 204 (21.1%).
For no topic did the results of the appeal and adjudication process affect the ranking of submissions on F1 .
The appeals documents were not anonymized before being submitted to the Topic Authority for final adjudication

kp.k: OCR quality limits retrieval and real-world generalizability
kp.d: Relevant documents missed by every team had lower mean dictionary-based OCR scores than retrieved relevant documents on all three Interactive topics. Restricting evaluation to better-OCR subsets generally raised recall while leaving precision comparatively stable and F1 rankings unchanged. At an OCR threshold of 0.85, H5’s Topic 103 recall was 0.786, precision 0.830 and F1 0.808. These are subset-based estimates, not observed improvements from repairing the entire collection. The authors describe their analysis as rough-and-ready and note that contemporary litigation collections were expected to be predominantly born-digital.
qs: the OCR quality of relevant documents that have been found by at least one team tends to be better than the OCR quality of relevant documents that have been missed by all teams.
precision is for the most part not affected by the quality of the OCR
Our analysis has been a deliberately rough-and-ready one, and it could certainly be followed up with additional research and analysis.
the relative rankings based on F1 do not change.

kp.k: Human assessment remains a substantial resource constraint
kp.d: Partial 2008 assessor surveys reported 631.15 hours reviewing 13,543 documents, equivalent to 21.5 documents per hour, compared with 25 in 2006 and 20 in 2007. The authors conclude that adding the highly relevant category did not substantially affect assessment speed. Volunteer capacity nevertheless constrained evaluation, making cost-effective sampling increasingly urgent. No Interactive participant undertook a completely manual review, so the exercise does not establish comparative performance against an end-to-end manual-review entrant.
qs: assessors reported that it took a collective 631.15 hours to review 13,543 documents, or a rate of 21.5 documents per hour.
it appears that the new highly relevant category did not substantially affect the assessment rate.
No participant undertook a completely manual review (although that would be permissible).
As we approach the limit of what relevance assessment by volunteers can support, cost-effective sampling is a matter of increasing urgency.

kp.k: Courts linked retrieval research with defensible discovery protocols
kp.d: The paper reports that Victor Stanley v. Creative Pipe discussed TREC in 2008 when addressing inadequate searching for potentially privileged documents. Judge Grimm expressed an expectation that research would identify reliable, economical methods and practices supporting arguments that a search was reasonable. The authors distinguish that judicial expectation from established results and situate the opinion within growing judicial attention to sophisticated retrieval and collaborative protocols following the December 2006 Federal Rules amendments.
qs: The goal of the project is to create industry best practices for use in electronic discovery.
Whether or not the results of the TREC Legal Track to date can be said to meet the judiciary’s expectations
These cases have arisen in the aftermath of the changes to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure involving “electronically stored information” that went into effect in December 2006.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Oard, Hedin, Tomlinson and Baron report that automated retrieval can outperform negotiated Boolean searches in e-discovery, but performance depends on the approach, topic, attorney guidance and document quality.
pts.d: The source concerns information retrieval and automated classification, not contemporary generative AI. Its concrete findings are that some automated approaches surpassed the Boolean benchmark in the 2008 Ad Hoc task; Boolean searches missed material as well as tangential evidence; and effective interaction with the attorney defining relevance can support high recall and precision. Relevance-feedback systems did not generally outperform baselines. The authors present these as findings about document retrieval, not predictions of lawyer replacement or legal-market restructuring. They also argue that poor OCR depresses recall and that human relevance assessments require quality control.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on TREC 2008 benchmark experiments, sampled human relevance judgments, adjudication and exploratory analyses, rather than measured market or employment outcomes.
pts.d: The collection contained 6,910,192 document records. The Ad Hoc task received 64 runs from 10 teams, with 26 topics usable for all-relevant scoring and 24 for highly relevant scoring. The highest mean estimated F1 at the submitted cutoff was 0.220, compared with 0.161 for the final negotiated Boolean reference. The relevance-feedback comparison covered 12 topics and found median F1 of 0.06 for feedback runs versus 0.09 for baseline runs and 0.14 for the Boolean reference. The Interactive task involved four teams and three topics. On Topic 103 alone, H5 achieved estimated post-adjudication recall of 0.624, precision of 0.810 and F1 of 0.705. Attorney-interaction time correlated with F1 among active submissions (r = 0.927), but the authors note the small number of observations and missing middle-range interaction times. Of 966 appealed assessments, 762 were overturned; these were selected appeals, not an overall human error-rate estimate. OCR-subset analyses supported the claim that poor text rendering limits recall. No participant conducted a completely manual review, so the experiment does not establish superiority over a wholly manual workflow.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern the 2008 experiments and are expressly qualified by topic breadth, retrieval limits, assessment uncertainty, unequal resources and atypical OCR quality.
pts.d: The authors compare the 2008 results with the 2006–2007 track and discuss further work in 2009, without a timetable for profession-wide automation. They do not attribute improved performance solely to allowing systems to choose their retrieval cutoff: 2008 topics were substantially broader, and Boolean negotiation performance could vary. Six Ad Hoc topics had more estimated relevant documents than the 100,000-document submission limit permitted participants to return. Individual-topic estimates could have substantial sampling error. The highly relevant category lacked training data and still required agreement studies. Interactive participants differed in methods, resources, attorney-interaction time and topic coverage; H5's strong outcome was on one topic, not a general vendor-wide performance estimate. The approximately 80% recall-and-precision result applies to an OCR-filtered subset rather than the full collection. The authors describe OCR adjustment as exploratory and caution that the scanned-document collection differs from contemporary born-digital discovery collections.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected users are litigation and regulatory-discovery teams, their corporate clients, senior attorneys, document reviewers and e-discovery providers.
pts.d: The authors frame automated retrieval as helping identify business records while balancing exhaustiveness against unnecessary human-review costs. The Ad Hoc task models selecting document sets for subsequent human review; the Interactive task models classifying the collection according to a responsible attorney's definition of responsiveness. Senior attorneys remain responsible for defining relevance, clarifying instructions and resolving appealed assessments. Researchers and e-discovery providers are expected to translate that guidance into effective retrieval methods. Human assessors supply and help correct the benchmark judgments. Potential cost-effectiveness and better discovery practice are motivations, but the paper does not quantify client savings, staffing reductions, fee changes or access-to-justice effects. Judicial optimism quoted in the introduction is contextual authority, not an independently established author finding that these methods satisfy legal obligations.
